description: FlameSense AI is an independent initiative led by a technology enthusiast and aspiring data science practitioner, exploring the intersection of AI, data science and space research. The project aims to transform complex NASA microgravity combustion research into meaningful insights through intelligent technology, interactive data visualization and innovation, contributing to a better understanding of fire safety for future space exploration.
summary:
**FlameSense AI** is an interactive research-exploration dashboard developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, responding to the *Flame in Freefall* challenge.

The project aims to make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to discover, compare and interpret. The prototype organises selected research from three NASA programmes—BASS, SAFFIRE and ACME—into a structured catalogue. Users can search by keyword, filter by research area, view a dynamic chart, compare programme summaries and explore programme-specific insights.

By bringing selected research information into one accessible interface, FlameSense AI provides a starting point for understanding combustion experiments and their relevance to fire safety in human space exploration.

The current prototype uses three manually curated programme records and rule-based insights. It does not yet use a trained machine-learning model, ingest live NASA data or predict fire behaviour. Future development will focus on expanding the catalogue, improving source traceability and introducing carefully scoped AI-assisted analysis.
details:
FlameSense AI is an interactive research-exploration dashboard designed to make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to discover, navigate, compare and interpret.

NASA has conducted numerous combustion experiments in microgravity, covering different fuel types, flame behaviours, material properties and fire-related phenomena. However, relevant information is distributed across research programmes, investigations and publications. Finding related information and understanding its relevance can be challenging, particularly for users who are not specialists in combustion science.

FlameSense AI addresses this challenge by organizing selected research information into a structured catalogue. The current prototype includes three NASA research programmes:

  • BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids): Research into the burning and extinction behaviour of solid fuels in microgravity.
  • SAFFIRE (Spacecraft Fire Experiments): Experiments investigating flame growth and fire behaviour aboard uncrewed spacecraft.
  • ACME (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments): A collection of gaseous combustion investigations, including the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), which examines material flammability relevant to spacecraft fire prevention.

The dashboard provides four main areas of functionality:

  1. About the Project: Introduces the project, its purpose and research scope.
  2. Research Explorer: Allows users to search the catalogue using keywords, filter by research area and view a dynamically updated chart.
  3. Programme Comparison: Presents selected research programmes side by side to make their objectives and research areas easier to compare.
  4. Research Insights: Provides concise, programme-specific insights using predefined rules based on the curated research information.

The current implementation uses a manually curated dataset and rule-based logic to organize and present information. It is an initial working prototype rather than a complete NASA research database or a trained machine-learning system.


FlameSense AI aims to reduce the effort required to navigate information about microgravity combustion research.

Its key benefits include:

  • Bringing selected research programme information together in one accessible interface.
  • Making research easier to discover through keyword search and research-area filtering.
  • Supporting side-by-side comparisons of different combustion research programmes.
  • Presenting concise insights that help users understand the focus and relevance of selected investigations.
  • Providing a structured starting point for further research, learning and investigation.
  • Making complex research information more approachable for students, researchers and non-specialist audiences.

The longer-term vision is to support a more accessible and connected understanding of combustion research relevant to human space exploration.

A better understanding of how materials burn, how flames behave in microgravity and how combustion can be suppressed is important to ongoing research into spacecraft fire safety.

FlameSense AI aims to help users navigate this body of knowledge and identify potentially relevant research more efficiently. It could eventually support researchers, students and space-technology communities in exploring evidence, identifying connections between investigations and developing further research questions.

The project is intended as a research-discovery and knowledge-navigation tool. It does not currently assess spacecraft fire risk, determine material safety or predict fire behaviour.

The prototype was developed using:

  • Python: Core programming language for data handling, filtering, comparison and application logic.
  • Google Colab: Cloud-based notebook environment for development and execution.
  • Gradio: Framework used to build the interactive web dashboard and its four functional tabs.
  • Pandas: Used for organizing and manipulating the structured research catalogue.
  • Plotly: Used to generate interactive, dynamically updated data visualizations.
  • HTML: Used to format the programme comparison presentation within the dashboard.
  • Google Drive: Used to organize and maintain project files, research materials, documentation and backups.

NASA research programme information and related scientific references informed the manually curated catalogue.

The current prototype does not require specialized hardware. It was developed using a standard computer and cloud-based development tools.

The creative aspect of FlameSense AI lies in combining research discovery, structured comparison and accessible visual presentation in one interface.

Rather than simply presenting separate summaries of NASA programmes, the project brings selected information into a consistent catalogue and provides different ways to explore it.

Its approach combines:

  • Search-driven research discovery.
  • Research-area filtering.
  • Dynamic visualisation of matching records.
  • Side-by-side programme comparison.
  • Programme-specific, rule-based insights.

The project also distinguishes between different types of combustion research instead of treating all microgravity combustion investigations as directly related to spacecraft fire safety. For example, it recognises that the Burning Rate Emulator is the ACME investigation specifically concerned with material flammability for spacecraft fire prevention.

This distinction helps preserve scientific context while making the information easier to navigate.


Several considerations guided the development of FlameSense AI:

Scientific accuracy: The research programmes have different objectives and experimental contexts. Their descriptions were structured to preserve these distinctions and avoid overstating their relevance to spacecraft fire safety.

Accessibility: The interface was designed to make selected research information easier to explore without requiring users to navigate multiple sources independently.

Transparency: The prototype uses manually curated records and predefined rules. Its current capabilities and limitations are explicitly identified rather than presenting rule-based insights as machine-generated scientific conclusions.

Usability: The four-tab dashboard separates project information, research exploration, programme comparison and research insights into clear functional areas.

Data scope and quality: The initial catalogue is deliberately limited to three selected programme-level records. Expanding it will require additional research, source verification and consistent data structuring.

Future scalability: The project structure allows for future expansion through additional research records, source-level links, improved relevance ranking and carefully scoped AI-assisted analysis.

Responsible interpretation: The dashboard is intended to support research discovery and understanding, not replace scientific expertise or provide operational spacecraft fire-safety decisions.

Conclusion

FlameSense AI establishes an initial foundation for making microgravity combustion research more discoverable and understandable. By combining structured research information with interactive exploration, comparison and rule-based insights, the project demonstrates how a focused digital tool can help bridge the gap between scientific information and accessible research knowledge.
